contributions: Systematic catalog of 18 classical graph analysis concepts spanning random graph models, centrality measures, network motifs, graphlet-based features, and graph kernels
Quantitative comparison of Erdős–Rényi, Barabási–Albert, and real network properties using the Karate Club graph as a running example
Explanation of how the Weisfeiler-Lehman kernel serves as a theoretical expressiveness ceiling for GNNs
limitations: Three fundamental limitations of hand-crafted features are identified: task-specificity (features must be redesigned per task), non-adaptivity (features ignore target labels), and combinatorial explosion (graphlet counting is intractable beyond k=5 nodes). Additionally, both ER and BA models fail to capture the simultaneous high clustering and short path length of real small-world networks, and betweenness/closeness centrality require careful handling in disconnected graphs.
methods: The chapter surveys classical graph feature engineering techniques rather than presenting new empirical experiments. It defines random graph baselines (ER and BA models), derives centrality measures (eigenvector, betweenness, closeness), introduces motif and graphlet-based descriptors including the 73-dimensional Graphlet Degree Vector, and presents graph kernels (graphlet kernel and Weisfeiler-Lehman kernel) for graph similarity computation. Link prediction is addressed via Katz similarity. Computations are demonstrated using NetworkX on the Zachary Karate Club graph.
results: The Karate Club graph has average clustering coefficient 0.571 versus the ER baseline of ~0.14. Maximum degree is 17, average path length is 2.41, and average degree is 4.59—highlighting the gap from random graph models. Eigenvector centrality for node 0 (instructor) is 0.356 and node 33 (president) is 0.313, with betweenness scores of 0.437 and 0.304 respectively. The WL kernel runs in O(nm) time versus O(n^k) for graphlet enumeration. Erdős–Rényi matches path lengths but dramatically underestimates clustering, while the Barabási–Albert model produces realistic hubs but also underestimates clustering.
tldr: This chapter establishes the classical graph feature engineering toolkit—random graph models, centrality measures, graphlets, and graph kernels—that preceded GNNs, while demonstrating why hand-crafted features are fundamentally limited by task-specificity, non-adaptivity, and combinatorial explosion.
